bridges.mechanism: An increase in maritime_attack_intensit raises energy/transport volatility and macroeconomic uncertainty, complicating central banks' inflation and growth forecasts and therefore increasing perceived monetary policy risk and uncertainty about timing/intensity of interventions.

A spike in maritime attacks crystallizes national‑security narratives and evidentiary links to hostile actors, prompting governments (especially the US) to tighten export controls, sanctions screening and security‑related AI policy toward China.

Sustained attacks increase insurance and operational risk for transoceanic hardware deployments, incentivizing corporations and states to accelerate capital deployment into onshore/regional cloud and AI infrastructure as a resilience/decoupling response.

Visible increases in missile/drone/small-boat attacks in the Russia‑Ukraine theatre produce a demonstration and tactics-transfer effect that accelerates adoption of similar maritime attack patterns by regional actors (including proxies), raising the rate of hostile incidents in the US–Iran maritime theatre.

A rise in effective maritime drone strikes around Ukraine prompts U.S. and allied naval commanders to expand interdiction and inspection operations (rules-of-engagement and patrols) to preempt drone-arms transfers and protect shipping in the Gulf, raising interdiction intensity.

An increase in shipping_transit_volume boosts trade activity and trade-finance settlements and reduces shipping/insurance risk premia, prompting higher cross-border portfolio and trade-related capital flows into affected corridors and instruments.

Sustained drops in commercial transit through key routes force exporters and importers to set up bilateral clearing arrangements and routings outside standard correspondent‑bank pipelines, accelerating adoption and integration of non‑SWIFT/alternative payment channels.

Sustained rerouting of commercial traffic away from Black Sea/Ukraine routes increases demand on alternative global corridors (Suez/Strait of Hormuz), mechanically raising crude and oil-product volumes transiting those chokepoints.
An increase in grain_export_flow eases global food supply concerns and lowers forward food-price risk, causing market and survey inflation expectations to decline over the near term.

A rise in fuel_supply_flow (i.e., restored/greater fuel shipments through the region) lowers wholesale and transport fuel prices, causing realized inflation to come in below prior market forecasts and thus reducing the inflation surprise rate.

Acute reductions in regional fuel shipments raise import bills and energy-price volatility for fuel‑importing BRICS economies, worsening current‑account balances and prompting exchange‑rate pressure and short‑term capital outflows.

Interruptions or reductions in maritime fuel flows raise energy and logistics constraints for fabs (fuel for generators, transport of specialty chemicals and tooling), forcing production curtailments or delayed ramp‑ups and thus lowering semiconductor output capacity.

Direct disruptions or reductions in fuel/fuel-product shipments from the Black Sea–Russia region tighten global physical supply and prompt a risk/supply premium in international crude benchmarks, lifting prices within weeks.

A decline in chokepoint_throughput (fewer barrels/day transiting key straits) produces an immediate physical supply shortfall for refined fuels in consuming markets, causing energy and transport components of CPI to print above forecasts and raising the inflation surprise rate.

A sharp drop in throughput through key chokepoints raises trade frictions and insurance/premia costs for exporters and importers in BRICS, triggering currency pressure and episodic capital flight as markets reprice external‑trade risks.

A drop in throughput through key Gulf chokepoints reallocates global tanker and bulk shipping capacity and spikes freight and insurance costs, prompting carriers to avoid higher‑risk routes and reducing the effective volume and reliability of Black Sea grain exports to global markets.

A drop in chokepoint throughput causes immediate shipment delays, higher freight and insurance costs for data‑center equipment, and project timelines slippage, which leads investors and operators to postpone or reduce AI infrastructure deployments and lower near‑term investment flows.

An escalation in maritime_interdiction (more frequent interdiction operations) raises regional geopolitical and trade risk, prompting non‑resident investors to withdraw portfolio capital from exposed markets and reallocate into safe‑haven assets, reducing net cross‑border inflows.

Sustained interdiction by US or US-backed forces raises perceived vulnerability of dollar-cleared maritime trade, pushing BRICS central banks and major exporters to accelerate deployment and bilateral use of non‑SWIFT/alternative settlement channels to preserve trade flows.

Sustained increases in US–Iran maritime interdiction drive US/NATO naval and air assets to redeploy toward the Gulf, creating temporary gaps in Western maritime presence and deterrence in the Black Sea that Russia can exploit to raise the tempo of attacks on shipping there.

A sustained increase in hostile_incident_rate (more attacks/seizures) heightens uncertainty about the persistence of supply disruptions and growth impacts, complicating central bank reaction functions and increasing perceived uncertainty about the timing and intensity of monetary policy.

A higher rate of attacks and seizures creates immediate operational disruptions that incentivize states and firms within BRICS to build and fund covert logistics, opaque intermediaries, and legal/financial workarounds to keep sanctioned or at‑risk trade moving.

Repeated hostile maritime incidents increase perceived reliance risk on Western security frameworks, prompting BRICS governments to deepen military-diplomatic and logistical ties with alternative security partners to diversify protection of sea lines of communication.

A spike in hostile incidents against shipping attributable to the US–Iran standoff incentivizes Iran (and its proxies) to accelerate transfer and operational support of UAVs to Russia as reciprocal leverage, enabling higher drone strike rates in the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

A rising rate of hostile maritime incidents creates a near-term national‑security pretext that prompts U.S. policymakers to tighten export controls and related regulatory measures against competitors, increasing overall regulatory stringency in the U.S.–China tech rivalry.

A sharp rise in benchmark_crude_price raises headline inflation and worsens fiscal balances in net‑importing sovereigns, pushing investors to demand higher yields (and often steepening the curve) to compensate for higher inflation and fiscal risk.

Faster AI model development yields improved maritime-domain awareness and automated target-tracking/decision-support, enabling US forces to detect, classify and task interdiction assets more frequently against Iranian vessels and proxy actors.

Heightened US–China tech rivalry drives large, time‑sensitive capital allocations into cloud and data‑center projects in particular jurisdictions, producing observable net cross‑border portfolio and project flows as investors move funds to host countries and away from sanctioned or higher‑risk jurisdictions.

A rapid uptick in AI infrastructure spending raises near‑term demand for construction, power, semiconductors and logistics, tightening capacity in those markets and causing realized inflation to overshoot prevailing forecasts.

Sustained flows of Chinese or China-led AI/cloud infrastructure investment into BRICS and partner states create economic dependencies, procurement ties, and regulatory harmonization that translate into quicker diplomatic and strategic alignment toward alternative blocs.

An uptick in AI and sensor infrastructure funding tied to the US–China tech competition accelerates deployment of persistent drones, sensors and C2 links in the region, increasing the tempo and geographic scope of US-led interdiction patrols versus Iranian maritime activity.

Expansion of chip fabrication and packaging capacity relieves supply‑side bottlenecks for electronics and intermediate goods, lowering goods price pressures and reducing realized inflation relative to expectations.

A measurable increase in domestic semiconductor production capacity provides alternative supply for critical chips, enabling targeted economies to run indigenous hardware stacks and routing/telecom infrastructure that bypasses vendors subject to export controls, directly boosting their ability to evade hardware-dependent sanctions.

A rise in global semiconductor output lowers procurement constraints for flight‑control, guidance and comms chips (including via third‑country suppliers), enabling faster production and deployment of inexpensive UAVs and loitering munitions that increase the rate of drone strikes against maritime and near‑shore targets.

Sudden increases in AI regulatory stringency create policy and earnings uncertainty (about productivity, investment, and fiscal impacts), complicating central‑bank outlooks and raising perceived uncertainty about the timing and intensity of monetary responses.

Sharper export controls and restrictive tech-related regulations from the U.S. and allies raise perceived exposure to Western payment/finance systems, prompting BRICS actors to accelerate adoption and integration of alternative cross‑border payment rails to reduce dependency and transactional surveillance.

Escalating tech‑export controls and related compliance measures driven by US–China rivalry raise transaction, insurance and diversion‑risk costs for shippers and traders dealing with the region, causing reduced tanker calls and a measurable drop in refined fuel shipments through contested maritime routes.

Higher expected future inflation increases uncertainty about long-run project economics and operating costs for capex‑heavy fabs, causing firms and investors to defer or slow new semiconductor capacity expansions.

Heightened uncertainty about major central bank policy increases perceived geopolitical economic risk and prompts BRICS policymakers to seek more reliable credit, trade and diplomatic partners, accelerating shifts toward alternative strategic alignments.

Elevated uncertainty about the timing/intensity of monetary-policy moves tightens venture and corporate financing conditions and risk appetite, reducing funding for compute‑intensive model development and slowing the pace of new large model projects.

A sustained rise in advanced‑economy sovereign yields raises the cost and volatility of dollar/Western funding, incentivising BRICS banks and states to accelerate integration of non‑Western payment rails and bilateral clearing arrangements to lower transaction and funding risk.

Rising sovereign yields increase the cost of trade finance and ship refinancing, prompting carriers and charterers to cancel sailings or withdraw capacity and thereby reduce commercial transit volume through the region.

A material rise in sovereign yields raises trade finance and shipping borrowing costs and insurance premia, causing some chartering and trade flows to be delayed or reduced and lowering volumetric flows through strategic chokepoints.

Sharp net capital outflows driven by a bond/inflation shock drain FX reserves and liquidity in BRICS markets, producing exchange‑rate pressure and forcing emergency capital controls or large nominal depreciations that reduce currency and capital stability.

A decline in cross-border capital flows reduces shipowners' and insurers' liquidity to pay for private security, higher-risk routing or elevated premiums, leaving vessels more exposed and increasing the rate of maritime attacks.

A fall in net cross‑border capital flows after an inflation shock limits foreign equity and project financing for data‑center builds and cloud rollouts, directly reducing additions to operational data‑center capacity.

Sudden capital outflows from oil‑importing countries weaken local currencies and constrain import financing, leading to reduced crude and product liftings and lower tanker transits through key chokepoints.

A sudden inflation surprise raises immediate input costs (construction, energy, services) and forces firms and cloud providers to reprioritize capex, prompting near-term delays or downsizing of AI infrastructure investments.

A larger-than-expected inflation print prompts investors and traders to buy commodities as an inflation hedge and prompts oil producers/traders to price in higher input costs, driving up spot and futures crude benchmarks in the near term.

A sudden rise in sanctions intensity restricts imports of critical goods and intermediate inputs, causing abrupt supply-side price shocks that push realized inflation above prevailing market forecasts.

Higher sanctions intensity that restricts exports of specialized chips, cloud services, and cross‑border research collaborations directly reduces available compute, toolchains, and external partnerships, slowing the pace of designing, training and releasing new large AI models.

Faster integration of alternative payment rails fragments global settlement corridors and increases frictions for traditional investors and custodians, reducing net cross-border portfolio and bond flows into conventional markets.

Integration of alternative cross-border payment rails lowers transaction frictions for buyers and shippers excluded from mainstream finance, restoring commercial contracts and thereby increasing chartering and transit flows through maritime chokepoints once payment clearing is operational.

Greater integration of alternative payment and settlement systems lowers cross‑border transaction frictions and counterparty risk for BRICS and allied investors, enabling faster and larger capital deployment into physical and cloud AI infrastructure in participating jurisdictions.

Deterioration in exchange-rate stability and accelerated capital flight raises sovereign risk and liquidity premia, driving up yields across maturities and often steepening the term structure as investors demand compensation for currency and rollover risk.

Expanded sanctions-evasion networks (front companies, reflagging, shadow brokers) enable sanctioned fuel cargoes to be rechartered, transshipped and insured through third-party intermediaries, increasing actual fuel shipments through regional routes.

Improved evasion capacity allows agricultural exporters to use middlemen, opaque paperwork and re-routing via permissive ports, raising the volume of grain shipments reaching international buyers despite formal restrictions.

Improved sanctions‑evasion capacity—via procurement intermediaries, gray‑market logistics and substitute supply chains—allows sanctioned fabs and buyers to obtain critical equipment and inputs, permitting maintenance or incremental expansion of semiconductor production capacity despite formal controls.

Improved BRICS-enabled sanctions‑evasion networks (shadow shipping services, ship-to-ship transfers, and opaque brokerage) allow more Iranian crude to reach buyers, directly increasing volumes transiting strategic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz.

A rapid shift toward alternative geopolitical alignments alters reserve usage, trade invoicing and bilateral financial arrangements, creating strategic uncertainty about central-bank interventions, reserve management and capital-control responses and thus raising perceived monetary policy risk.

A visible shift by BRICS toward alternative geopolitical alignments prompts the US and allied governments to broaden export controls, investment screening and AI oversight on tech ties with aligned partners, increasing regulatory stringency in the US–China tech rivalry.

A faster BRICS-alignment by Iran's partners (training, arms transfers, intelligence sharing and diplomatic backing) increases Iran's operational capacity and political willingness to conduct or authorize more maritime harassment and seizures in the Gulf, raising the rate of hostile incidents.

nodes.label: Black Sea Escalation: Maritime Attacks, Drone Warfare, and Global Supply Risks
Maritime attack intensity
nodes.description: The aggregate rate and severity of hostile actions directed at maritime targets in the regional sea space (including missiles, drones and small-boat attacks).

nodes.label: Drone strike frequency
nodes.description: The temporal frequency of unmanned aerial vehicle strikes affecting maritime infrastructure, vessels, or nearshore facilities.

nodes.label: Naval defensive alertness
nodes.description: The readiness level and responsiveness of naval and maritime air defenses deployed in the operational theater.

nodes.label: Port operational capacity
nodes.description: The proportion of port handling, storage and loading/unloading capability that is available and functioning.

nodes.label: Shipping transit volume
nodes.description: The flow rate of commercial maritime transits through the regional chokepoints measured as number or tonnage per time unit.

nodes.label: Grain export flow
nodes.description: The throughput rate of agricultural commodity shipments (grain) leaving the region toward international markets.

nodes.label: Fuel supply flow
nodes.description: The flow rate of refined fuel and energy product shipments through regional maritime routes and terminals.

nodes.label: Perceived risk of vessel seizure
nodes.description: The perceived likelihood among mariners and shippers that commercial vessels may be interdicted, detained or seized on regional waters.

nodes.label: Conventional escalation risk
nodes.description: The overall perceived probability that maritime incidents will broaden into higher-level conventional military confrontation.

nodes.label: Arms proliferation rate
nodes.description: The rate at which weapons, delivery systems, or enabling technologies are arriving, circulating, or being replicated within the theater.

nodes.label: Maritime insurance costs
nodes.description: The prevailing premium levels and insurance-related surcharges applied to commercial shipping operating in the region.

nodes.label: Port infrastructure damage
nodes.description: The accumulated extent of physical damage to port terminals, storage facilities and onshore logistics assets that reduces functionality.

nodes.label: Diplomatic pressure intensity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of diplomatic actions aimed at changing maritime behavior, protecting shipping, or de-escalating tensions.

nodes.label: Market price volatility
nodes.description: The short-to-medium-term variability in international commodity and fuel prices attributable to regional supply and transit disruptions.

nodes.label: Logistics rerouting rate
nodes.description: The rate at which cargo flows are redirected from affected maritime routes to alternative corridors (rail, road, other ports).

nodes.label: Surveillance coverage density
nodes.description: The spatial density and persistence of maritime and aerial surveillance assets covering shipping lanes and ports.

Hormuz blockade and regional attacks choking global oil supply
Chokepoint throughput
nodes.description: The volumetric rate of crude and oil-product cargo (barrels/day) transiting strategic maritime chokepoints.

nodes.label: Tanker transit rate
nodes.description: The number of oil tankers and related cargo vessels passing through key sea lanes per unit time.

nodes.label: Spare production capacity
nodes.description: The volume of additional oil production that can be brought online within a defined short-to-medium timeframe.

nodes.label: Global supply gap
nodes.description: The net difference between globally available oil supply and aggregate demand at prevailing conditions.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization
nodes.description: The proportion of global refining capacity that is actively processing crude into products at a given time.

nodes.label: Commercial inventories
nodes.description: The aggregated level of commercial crude and product stocks held in storage facilities and terminals.

nodes.label: Marine insurance premia
nodes.description: The average war-risk, hull and other voyage insurance premium levels charged for tanker voyages in affected waters.

nodes.label: Shipping freight rate
nodes.description: The freight cost per ton (or per barrel) for transporting crude and refined products by sea.

nodes.label: Maritime interdiction intensity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of naval and quasi‑naval operations that obstruct or control maritime transit.

nodes.label: Hostile incident rate
nodes.description: The rate of armed attacks, strikes, seizures or hostile events directed at shipping and maritime infrastructure.

nodes.label: Export rerouting share
nodes.description: The proportion of export volumes diverted from primary sea routes to alternative pipelines, terminals or passages.

nodes.label: Average transit delay
nodes.description: The mean additional time incurred per voyage due to inspections, rerouting, congestion or security measures.

nodes.label: Benchmark crude price
nodes.description: The prevailing market reference price level for crude oil (e.g., international benchmark) in currency per barrel.

nodes.label: Market supply expectations
nodes.description: The prevailing collective expectation in markets about future supply–demand balance and tightness over the forecasting horizon.

nodes.label: Demand destruction rate
nodes.description: The rate at which oil consumption declines in response to price increases, economic slowdown or access constraints.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve drawdown rate
nodes.description: The rate at which government and strategic reserves are released or withdrawn into the market.

nodes.label: Stalled Iran–US talks keep Hormuz closed
Escalation of Houthi attacks in Red Sea
Ship oil leak and salvage off Oman
Saudi expansion of Mediterranean pipeline exports
Major oil firms resume Venezuelan activity
AI infrastructure boom, finance & geopolitical competition
AI compute demand
nodes.description: The aggregate level of demand for machine‑learning compute resources across training and inference workloads.

nodes.label: AI model development rate
nodes.description: The pace at which new or larger machine‑learning models are designed, trained, and released.

nodes.label: Infrastructure investment flow
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of financial capital being deployed into physical and cloud AI infrastructure over time.

nodes.label: Market valuation level
nodes.description: The collective valuation metrics and price levels applied to firms and assets associated with the AI ecosystem.

nodes.label: Financial leverage level
nodes.description: The degree of debt, credit exposure, and structured financing tied to AI infrastructure and related assets.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain capacity
nodes.description: The available throughput and flexibility of logistics, component suppliers, and material inputs supporting AI hardware production.

nodes.label: Semiconductor production capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate output potential of chip fabrication and packaging capacity relevant to AI accelerators.

nodes.label: Data‑center operational capacity
nodes.description: The installed and operable compute, storage, and networking resources in data centers available for AI workloads.

nodes.label: AI energy demand
nodes.description: The total energy consumption attributable to AI compute and model operations, measured as a system‑level demand for power.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity vulnerability level
nodes.description: The prevalence and severity of exploitable weaknesses in AI systems, models, and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Biosecurity risk potential
nodes.description: The likelihood and potential impact of biological misuse or hazardous outputs facilitated by AI tools and models.

nodes.label: Skilled talent supply
nodes.description: The available pool and skill level of workers capable of building, operating, and securing AI systems.

nodes.label: Regulatory policy stringency
nodes.description: The strictness and breadth of regulatory and policy constraints applied to AI development, deployment, and related markets.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tech competition intensity
nodes.description: The level of strategic competition and state‑led industrial policy pressures focusing on technological capabilities and secure supply chains.

nodes.label: Open‑model adoption rate
nodes.description: The rate at which open‑weight or openly shared AI models and standards are adopted across developers and operators.

nodes.label: Operational incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of operational failures, outages, breaches, or other incidents affecting AI infrastructure and services.

nodes.label: Hyperscalers' large purchase commitments translate into orders
Escalating export controls and China–trade frictions
Corporate and regulatory safeguards after AI bio/cyber incidents
Foxconn global AI server production ramp
Adoption and trading of AI compute futures
Inflation data and central-bank uncertainty driving a bond-market repricing
Consumer-price inflation rate
nodes.description: The continuous percentage change in the general consumer price level over a specified rolling period.

nodes.label: Wholesale-price inflation rate
nodes.description: The continuous percentage change in wholesale or producer price indices over a specified rolling period.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and survey-implied anticipated future inflation rate over near-to-medium horizons.

nodes.label: Monetary policy uncertainty/risk
nodes.description: The perceived uncertainty about future monetary policy actions and their timing/intensity.

nodes.label: Policy-rate expectation
nodes.description: The expected path or level of short-term policy interest rates implied by markets and forecasts.

nodes.label: Sovereign yield term structure
nodes.description: The set of sovereign interest rates across maturities representing the level and slope of the yield curve.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: The component of long-term sovereign yields reflecting compensation for duration and uncertainty separate from expected short rates.

nodes.label: Safe-asset allocation
nodes.description: The share of investor portfolios allocated to assets perceived as safe or reserve-like at a point in time.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flow volumes
nodes.description: The net continuous flow of capital across borders driven by portfolio reallocation, foreign investment and hedging activity.

nodes.label: Sovereign bond supply flow
nodes.description: The ongoing issuance rate of sovereign debt securities into financial markets over a given period.

nodes.label: Market liquidity depth
nodes.description: The degree to which markets can absorb trades without large price moves, as measured by available depth and bid-ask tightness.

nodes.label: FX intervention intensity
nodes.description: The rate and magnitude of official foreign-exchange operations intended to influence exchange rates or market conditions.

nodes.label: Exchange-rate volatility
nodes.description: The realized or implied variability of exchange rates over a chosen time horizon.

nodes.label: Commodity price volatility
nodes.description: The realized or implied variability of major commodity prices (e.g., energy, metals) that affect inflation and trade balances.

nodes.label: Investor risk aversion
nodes.description: The prevailing degree of risk tolerance among investors, shaping demand for risky versus safe assets.

nodes.label: Inflation surprise rate
nodes.description: The continuous deviation between realized inflation data and prevailing market/forecast expectations.

nodes.label: BOJ decision and likely September hike
Sustained large US Treasury issuance and widening deficit
Iran's Economic Survival and Geopolitical Pivot under U.S. Pressure
Sanctions and economic pressure intensity
nodes.description: The overall severity and frequency of external economic coercion measures applied to the target economy (trade restrictions, asset freezes, financial exclusion).

nodes.label: Military escalation risk
nodes.description: The perceived probability and momentum of kinetic conflict widening or intensifying in the regional security environment.

nodes.label: Survival economy adaptation
nodes.description: The rate and depth at which informal exchanges, barter, rationing, and low-capital economic practices expand within the domestic economy.

nodes.label: Alternative payment system integration
nodes.description: The extent of integration with non-mainstream cross-border payment channels and alternative settlement arrangements.

nodes.label: Internal political control strength
nodes.description: The degree of centralized authority, coercive capacity, and institutional consolidation within the domestic political system.

nodes.label: Trade diversion rate
nodes.description: The flux of export and import volumes being reoriented away from traditional partners toward alternative trading relationships.

nodes.label: Currency and capital stability
nodes.description: The stability of the exchange rate and the net pace of capital flows, including capital flight and capital controls effectiveness.

nodes.label: Inflation and cost-of-living pressure
nodes.description: The trend level of consumer price increases and resulting real-income erosion experienced by households.

nodes.label: Household credit and payment-pattern shift
nodes.description: The rate at which consumers move toward deferred-payment, credit-based, or informal financing mechanisms for consumption.

nodes.label: Regional defense procurement demand
nodes.description: The aggregate demand growth for military and defense-related goods and services across neighboring states and markets.

nodes.label: Global commodity price volatility
nodes.description: The variance and sensitivity of major commodity prices (energy, metals, food) to shocks originating from the regional confrontation.

nodes.label: Cross-border financial cooperation level
nodes.description: The stock of formalized financial linkages and cooperative arrangements among alternative banking and development networks.

nodes.label: Sanctions evasion capacity
nodes.description: The capability and resources available to bypass external financial and trade restrictions (networks, intermediaries, workaround mechanisms).

nodes.label: Regime legitimacy perception
nodes.description: Popular and elite perceptions of the governing authority's legitimacy and its social mandate to govern.

nodes.label: Shift toward alternative geopolitical alignments
nodes.description: The rate at which the polity reorients diplomatic and strategic partnerships away from established networks toward alternative blocs or partners.

nodes.label: External diplomatic pressure signals
nodes.description: The intensity and clarity of non-economic diplomatic communications and demands from external actors directed at the polity.

Heightened uncertainty about major central bank policy increases perceived geopolitical economic risk and prompts BRICS policymakers to seek more reliable credit, trade and diplomatic partners, accelerating shifts toward alternative strategic alignments.

Elevated uncertainty about the timing/intensity of monetary-policy moves tightens venture and corporate financing conditions and risk appetite, reducing funding for compute‑intensive model development and slowing the pace of new large model projects.

A sustained rise in advanced‑economy sovereign yields raises the cost and volatility of dollar/Western funding, incentivising BRICS banks and states to accelerate integration of non‑Western payment rails and bilateral clearing arrangements to lower transaction and funding risk.

Rising sovereign yields increase the cost of trade finance and ship refinancing, prompting carriers and charterers to cancel sailings or withdraw capacity and thereby reduce commercial transit volume through the region.

A material rise in sovereign yields raises trade finance and shipping borrowing costs and insurance premia, causing some chartering and trade flows to be delayed or reduced and lowering volumetric flows through strategic chokepoints.

Sharp net capital outflows driven by a bond/inflation shock drain FX reserves and liquidity in BRICS markets, producing exchange‑rate pressure and forcing emergency capital controls or large nominal depreciations that reduce currency and capital stability.

A decline in cross-border capital flows reduces shipowners' and insurers' liquidity to pay for private security, higher-risk routing or elevated premiums, leaving vessels more exposed and increasing the rate of maritime attacks.

A fall in net cross‑border capital flows after an inflation shock limits foreign equity and project financing for data‑center builds and cloud rollouts, directly reducing additions to operational data‑center capacity.

Sudden capital outflows from oil‑importing countries weaken local currencies and constrain import financing, leading to reduced crude and product liftings and lower tanker transits through key chokepoints.

A sudden inflation surprise raises immediate input costs (construction, energy, services) and forces firms and cloud providers to reprioritize capex, prompting near-term delays or downsizing of AI infrastructure investments.

A larger-than-expected inflation print prompts investors and traders to buy commodities as an inflation hedge and prompts oil producers/traders to price in higher input costs, driving up spot and futures crude benchmarks in the near term.

A sudden rise in sanctions intensity restricts imports of critical goods and intermediate inputs, causing abrupt supply-side price shocks that push realized inflation above prevailing market forecasts.

Higher sanctions intensity that restricts exports of specialized chips, cloud services, and cross‑border research collaborations directly reduces available compute, toolchains, and external partnerships, slowing the pace of designing, training and releasing new large AI models.

Faster integration of alternative payment rails fragments global settlement corridors and increases frictions for traditional investors and custodians, reducing net cross-border portfolio and bond flows into conventional markets.

Integration of alternative cross-border payment rails lowers transaction frictions for buyers and shippers excluded from mainstream finance, restoring commercial contracts and thereby increasing chartering and transit flows through maritime chokepoints once payment clearing is operational.

Greater integration of alternative payment and settlement systems lowers cross‑border transaction frictions and counterparty risk for BRICS and allied investors, enabling faster and larger capital deployment into physical and cloud AI infrastructure in participating jurisdictions.

Deterioration in exchange-rate stability and accelerated capital flight raises sovereign risk and liquidity premia, driving up yields across maturities and often steepening the term structure as investors demand compensation for currency and rollover risk.

Expanded sanctions-evasion networks (front companies, reflagging, shadow brokers) enable sanctioned fuel cargoes to be rechartered, transshipped and insured through third-party intermediaries, increasing actual fuel shipments through regional routes.

Improved evasion capacity allows agricultural exporters to use middlemen, opaque paperwork and re-routing via permissive ports, raising the volume of grain shipments reaching international buyers despite formal restrictions.

Improved sanctions‑evasion capacity—via procurement intermediaries, gray‑market logistics and substitute supply chains—allows sanctioned fabs and buyers to obtain critical equipment and inputs, permitting maintenance or incremental expansion of semiconductor production capacity despite formal controls.

Improved BRICS-enabled sanctions‑evasion networks (shadow shipping services, ship-to-ship transfers, and opaque brokerage) allow more Iranian crude to reach buyers, directly increasing volumes transiting strategic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz.

A rapid shift toward alternative geopolitical alignments alters reserve usage, trade invoicing and bilateral financial arrangements, creating strategic uncertainty about central-bank interventions, reserve management and capital-control responses and thus raising perceived monetary policy risk.

A visible shift by BRICS toward alternative geopolitical alignments prompts the US and allied governments to broaden export controls, investment screening and AI oversight on tech ties with aligned partners, increasing regulatory stringency in the US–China tech rivalry.

A faster BRICS-alignment by Iran's partners (training, arms transfers, intelligence sharing and diplomatic backing) increases Iran's operational capacity and political willingness to conduct or authorize more maritime harassment and seizures in the Gulf, raising the rate of hostile incidents.
